category: Core vocabulary: cooking and the kitchen

entries.meaning: The room where food is stored, prepared, and cooked. ---
examples: We finally remodeled the kitchen last spring.
He was standing in the kitchen making coffee.
Most of the apartments in that building have tiny kitchens.

entries.meaning: The appliance with burners on top that you cook on. ---
examples: There's a pot of chili on the stove.
Don't leave the stove on when you go out.
Our old stove only has three burners that work.
entries.contrast: Americans say stove or range; British English says cooker.

entries.meaning: The closed compartment you bake or roast food in. ---
examples: Preheat the oven to 375.
The bread's been in the oven for forty minutes.
Both ovens died the week before Thanksgiving.
entries.contrast: Written with an o but said UH-vun, rhyming with the first part of 'lovin'.

entries.meaning: The appliance that keeps food cold. ---
examples: Put the milk back in the refrigerator.
The new refrigerator barely fit through the door.
Restaurant refrigerators run all night long.
entries.contrast: The short form fridge is spelled with a d that the full word doesn't have.

entries.meaning: An informal word for a refrigerator. ---
examples: There's nothing in the fridge but ketchup.
Stick the leftovers in the fridge.
We keep a second fridge out in the garage.

entries.meaning: The compartment or appliance that keeps food frozen. ---
examples: I've got a bag of peas in the freezer.
The freezer needs defrosting again.
Chest freezers hold a lot more than you'd think.

entries.meaning: An oven that heats food quickly with microwave radiation. ---
examples: Heat it in the microwave for two minutes.
Don't put anything metal in the microwave.
The dorm kitchen has two microwaves and one sink.

entries.meaning: A machine that washes dishes automatically. ---
examples: Can you load the dishwasher before you leave?
The dishwasher is making that noise again.
Older apartments here don't come with dishwashers.

entries.meaning: A small appliance that browns slices of bread. ---
examples: The toaster burns everything on setting five.
He dropped a bagel in the toaster and forgot about it.
We got two toasters as wedding gifts.

entries.meaning: A metal frame over a fire or gas flame for cooking food outdoors. ---
examples: Dad's out back firing up the grill.
We cooked the whole dinner on the grill.
The apartment complex has two grills by the pool.
entries.contrast: In American English a grill is the outdoor barbecue; the heating element inside a US oven is the broiler, which the British call a grill.

entries.meaning: The part of an oven that cooks food with heat from directly above. ---
examples: Put it under the broiler for two minutes to brown the top.
On this stove the broiler is the drawer underneath.
Watch it closely — broilers burn things in seconds.
entries.contrast: An American broiler is a British grill; an American grill is the outdoor kind.

entries.meaning: One of the cooking rings or elements on top of a stove. ---
examples: Move the pan to the back burner.
One burner on this stove never lights.
Turn the burner down before it boils over.

entries.meaning: The basin with a faucet where you wash dishes and hands. ---
examples: There's a stack of dishes in the sink.
Just rinse it off in the sink.
The kitchen has a double sink.

entries.meaning: The flat working surface along a kitchen wall. ---
examples: Wipe down the countertop when you're done.
Granite countertops were the big selling point.
Don't leave raw chicken sitting on the countertop.

entries.meaning: A cupboard with shelves and a door, usually mounted on a wall. ---
examples: The glasses are in the cabinet above the sink.
We painted the kitchen cabinets white.
He couldn't reach the top cabinet without a chair.
entries.contrast: In ordinary speech it collapses to two syllables: KAB-nut.

entries.meaning: A small room or closet where dry food is kept. ---
examples: There's a box of pasta in the pantry.
Our pantry is really just a closet with shelves.
Older houses around here have walk-in pantries.

entries.meaning: A sliding box built into a piece of furniture. ---
examples: The forks are in the top drawer.
That drawer sticks every single time.
He went through all the kitchen drawers looking for a corkscrew.
entries.contrast: One syllable in American speech — it sounds like 'draw' with an r, not DRAW-er.

entries.meaning: A frame of bars used to hold or cool things. ---
examples: Move the oven rack up one position.
Let the cookies cool on a wire rack.
The dish rack by the sink is always full.

entries.meaning: A device that crushes coffee, pepper, or spices into small pieces. ---
examples: Grind the beans fresh in a burr grinder.
There's a pepper grinder on every table.
Cheap grinders heat the coffee up too much.

entries.meaning: A device that counts down and signals when cooking time is up. ---
examples: Set a timer for twelve minutes.
The timer went off and nobody heard it.
I run two timers when I'm cooking three things at once.

entries.meaning: A device for weighing ingredients. ---
examples: A kitchen scale makes baking much more accurate.
Put the bowl on the scale and hit tare.
Digital scales are cheap now.
entries.contrast: One device is a scale, singular, even though Russian весы is plural.

entries.meaning: A deep round container with a handle for cooking on a stove. ---
examples: Bring a big pot of water to a boil.
She stirred the pot every few minutes.
All my pots are stacked in the bottom cabinet.

entries.meaning: A shallow metal container used for frying or baking. ---
examples: Heat a little oil in the pan.
Pour the batter into a greased pan.
Nonstick pans don't last forever.

entries.meaning: A heavy frying pan with sloping sides. ---
examples: Brown the onions in a cast-iron skillet.
He fried the eggs in the same skillet.
Those old skillets only get better with age.

entries.meaning: A small deep pan with a single long handle. ---
examples: Melt the butter in a small saucepan.
The rice is in the saucepan on the back burner.
I only own two saucepans.

entries.meaning: A deep bowl-shaped pan used for quick, high-heat cooking. ---
examples: Get the wok screaming hot before the vegetables go in.
A carbon steel wok costs about thirty bucks.
Most home stoves aren't hot enough for real wok cooking.

entries.meaning: A flat piece of metal, wood, or plastic used to carry or hold food. ---
examples: She carried the drinks out on a tray.
Line the tray with parchment first.
The ice trays are in the freezer door.

entries.meaning: A bowl full of holes used for draining water off food. ---
examples: Drain the pasta in a colander.
Rinse the beans in a colander under cold water.
We own two colanders and I can never find either one.

entries.meaning: A mesh device that separates solids from a liquid. ---
examples: Pour the stock through a fine-mesh strainer.
Use a strainer so the seeds don't get in.
Small strainers work better for loose tea.

entries.meaning: A fine mesh screen for sifting dry ingredients or straining liquids. ---
examples: Push the sauce through a sieve to make it smooth.
Sift the flour through a sieve first.
The finest sieves clog almost immediately.
entries.contrast: Rhymes with 'give' — SIV. The -ie- is not said 'ee'.

entries.meaning: A metal tool with sharp holes for shredding food. ---
examples: Shred the cheese on the coarse side of the grater.
A box grater is easier to clean than it looks.
Both graters went through the dishwasher.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like 'greater'.

entries.meaning: A hand tool that strips the skin off vegetables and fruit. ---
examples: Peel the carrots with a vegetable peeler.
A sharp peeler saves a lot of time.
Y-shaped peelers are the ones most cooks prefer.

entries.meaning: A loop-shaped wire tool for beating eggs or cream. ---
examples: Beat the eggs with a whisk.
Use a whisk, not a fork, or you'll get lumps.
Balloon whisks are the ones for whipping cream.

entries.meaning: A flat tool for flipping food or scraping a bowl. ---
examples: Flip the pancakes with a spatula.
Scrape the bowl down with a rubber spatula.
I keep three spatulas in the crock by the stove.

entries.meaning: A deep long-handled spoon for serving soup. ---
examples: Serve the soup with a ladle.
He filled each bowl with two ladles of chili.
The ladle is hanging on the hook by the stove.

entries.meaning: A utensil with a shallow bowl on a handle, used for eating and stirring. ---
examples: Stir it with a wooden spoon.
I need a clean spoon.
All the spoons are dirty.

entries.meaning: A utensil with prongs for picking up food. ---
examples: Test the potatoes with a fork.
He set a knife and fork at every place.
The forks go on the left.

entries.meaning: A small spoon, or the amount of an ingredient it holds. ---
examples: Add a teaspoon of vanilla.
That's about two teaspoons of salt.
Level the teaspoon off with the back of a knife.

entries.meaning: A large spoon, or the amount of an ingredient it holds. ---
examples: Melt two tablespoons of butter.
A tablespoon is three teaspoons.
Measure the oil with a real tablespoon, not a soup spoon.

entries.meaning: A cylinder used to flatten dough. ---
examples: Roll the dough out with a rolling pin.
Her rolling pin was her grandmother's.
Marble rolling pins stay cold, which helps with pastry.

entries.meaning: A long pin that holds pieces of food together for grilling. ---
examples: Thread the shrimp onto a skewer.
Soak wooden skewers first so they don't burn.
He pulled the meat off the skewer with his fork.

entries.meaning: A hollow container that gives food its shape as it sets. ---
examples: Pour the jelly into a mold and chill it overnight.
She turned the cake out of a bundt mold.
Silicone molds make it easy to get chocolate out.
entries.contrast: American spelling is mold; British English writes mould.

entries.meaning: A flat board you chop food on. ---
examples: Chop the onion on a cutting board, not on the counter.
Use a separate cutting board for raw meat.
Wooden cutting boards need oil once in a while.
entries.contrast: Americans say cutting board; British English says chopping board.

entries.meaning: A padded glove for handling hot pans. ---
examples: Grab an oven mitt before you touch that.
The mitt has a hole burned through the thumb.
Both mitts are in the drawer by the stove.

entries.meaning: A garment tied over your clothes to keep them clean while cooking. ---
examples: He tied on an apron before he started.
There's flour all over your apron.
The restaurant hands out clean aprons every shift.

entries.meaning: A soft absorbent block used for washing dishes and wiping surfaces. ---
examples: Wipe the counter with a damp sponge.
That sponge smells — just throw it out.
I buy sponges in packs of six.
entries.contrast: Written -onge but said SPUNJ, rhyming with 'plunge'.

entries.meaning: A soap-like cleaner used for washing dishes or clothes. ---
examples: Add a squirt of dish detergent to the water.
We're completely out of detergent.
The store-brand detergents work just as well.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: Thin sheet metal used to wrap or cover food. ---
examples: Cover the pan with foil and bake it another hour.
Wrap the potatoes in foil before they go on the grill.
We're out of foil — use parchment instead.
entries.contrast: Uncountable: a sheet of foil, never 'a foil' or 'foils' in the kitchen sense.

entries.meaning: Heat-resistant paper used to line baking pans. ---
examples: Line the sheet pan with parchment.
The cookies won't stick if you use parchment.
One roll of parchment lasts me a year.

entries.meaning: A large flat plate for serving food to several people. ---
examples: Arrange the cheese on a wooden platter.
He carried the turkey out on a big platter.
They sent over two platters of sandwiches.

entries.meaning: A piece of cloth or paper used at the table to wipe your hands and mouth. ---
examples: Grab a napkin — you've got sauce on your chin.
She folded a cloth napkin at each place.
The napkins are in the top drawer.

entries.meaning: A cloth spread over a table before a meal. ---
examples: Spread a tablecloth over the picnic table.
Somebody spilled wine on the tablecloth.
They save the good tablecloths for holidays.

entries.meaning: The knives, forks, and spoons used at a meal. ---
examples: Set out the silverware while I finish the salad.
There's silverware in the drawer by the sink.
He ran out of clean silverware halfway through the party.
entries.contrast: Uncountable — never 'a silverware' or 'silverwares'. British English says cutlery.

entries.meaning: Pots and pans considered together. ---
examples: They registered for a whole set of cookware.
Cast iron is the cheapest good cookware you can buy.
Most nonstick cookware can't go in the dishwasher.
entries.contrast: Uncountable, like equipment: a piece of cookware, never 'cookwares'.

entries.meaning: A tool used in preparing or eating food. ---
examples: Use a wooden utensil so you don't scratch the pan.
The drawer is jammed with utensils nobody ever uses.
Bring your own utensils to the picnic.
entries.contrast: Stress is on the second syllable: yoo-TEN-sul.

entries.meaning: A machine designed for a household job such as cooking or washing. ---
examples: The kitchen comes with all new appliances.
That appliance draws a lot of power.
They deliver large appliances on Tuesdays.

entries.meaning: A pair of thin sticks used for eating in much of East Asia. ---
examples: He still can't eat with chopsticks.
They gave us plastic forks instead of chopsticks.
A pair of chopsticks came with every order.
entries.contrast: Normally plural, since you use two: a pair of chopsticks.

entries.meaning: The activity of preparing food, or a particular style of it. ---
examples: He does most of the cooking at home.
Italian cooking uses far fewer ingredients than people think.
Cooking for eight people takes some planning.

entries.meaning: The activity of cooking bread, cakes, and pastry in an oven. ---
examples: She got into baking during the pandemic.
Baking is more exact than cooking — you can't just eyeball it.
He's much better at baking than at anything on the stove.

entries.meaning: The state of a liquid bubbling at its highest temperature. ---
examples: Bring the water to a boil before you add the pasta.
The soup came to a boil faster than I expected.
Turn it down as soon as you get a rolling boil.
entries.русский: кипение (в оборотах bring to a boil)

entries.meaning: Gentle cooking in liquid just below boiling. ---
examples: Reduce the heat and hold it at a simmer.
Bring the sauce to a simmer, then cover it.
A slow simmer pulls a lot more flavor out of the bones.
entries.русский: слабое кипение, томление на медленном огне

entries.meaning: A sauce of oil and vinegar or cream poured over salad. ---
examples: What kind of dressing do you want on your salad?
Toss the greens with the dressing right before you serve it.
The house dressings are all made from scratch.

entries.meaning: A seasoned liquid that food soaks in before cooking. ---
examples: Let the chicken sit in the marinade overnight.
The marinade is just soy sauce, garlic, and ginger.
Acidic marinades will start to cook the fish.
entries.contrast: The noun is marinade (MEH-ruh-nayd); the verb is marinate (MEH-ruh-nayt).

entries.meaning: A shiny coating brushed or poured over food. ---
examples: Brush a honey glaze over the ham.
The donuts have a thin sugar glaze.
Sweet glazes burn if the oven's too hot.

entries.meaning: Food put on top of another food for flavor. ---
examples: What toppings do you want on the pizza?
The crumb topping is the best part.
Extra toppings are a dollar each.

entries.meaning: One standard helping of food, as counted in a recipe. ---
examples: This recipe makes four servings.
One serving is around 300 calories.
He went back for a second serving.

entries.meaning: A style of cooking associated with a country or region. ---
examples: He's obsessed with Thai cuisine.
The restaurant serves modern American cuisine.
French cuisine isn't all heavy sauces.
entries.contrast: Said kwih-ZEEN: the c is a k sound and the s sounds like z.

entries.meaning: The sensation food produces in your mouth, or a small sample of it. ---
examples: It has a slightly bitter taste.
A bad cold ruins your sense of taste.
Give me a taste before you add more salt.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: The way food feels in the mouth. ---
examples: The bread has a nice chewy texture.
Overcooking ruins the texture of shrimp.
The two sauces have completely different textures.

entries.meaning: The level of warmth used to cook something. ---
examples: Cook it over medium heat.
Turn the heat down before it scorches.
Cast iron holds heat better than aluminum.

entries.meaning: The hot vapor that rises from boiling water. ---
examples: Lift the lid away from you so the steam doesn't burn you.
The rice finishes cooking in its own steam.
There was so much steam the windows fogged up.

entries.meaning: An amount of food made or baked at one time. ---
examples: The first batch of cookies burned.
She makes a big batch of soup on Sundays.
We froze two batches of sauce.

entries.meaning: Ingredients that have been combined together. ---
examples: Stir the mixture until it's smooth.
Pour the mixture over the crust.
Both mixtures need to chill for an hour.

entries.meaning: The colored outer part of citrus peel, grated for flavor. ---
examples: Add the zest of one lemon.
Orange zest makes the whole thing taste brighter.
Grate the zest off before you juice the fruit.

entries.meaning: A dish of small pieces cooked quickly over high heat while being stirred.
examples: We had a vegetable stir-fry for dinner.
A stir-fry takes about ten minutes start to finish.
Weeknight stir-fries are my go-to.
entries.русский: блюдо, обжаренное в воке на сильном огне
